Writing for Machines§01 / the point

A readme file is documentation for whoever installs it.

A context file is documentation for an agent that'll never remember you.Same skill. I’d been practising it for the last couple of years and didn’t know what for.

Writing for MachinesThe question§06 / how it gets captured

“How do you get
all that context
into one file?”

//

I didn't have an answer. So I went and read my own chat history.

//

The chats weren't random. They fell into a handful of shapes.the same few formats, over and over — I'd just never looked

//

The context goes in long before the first file exists. The artifact is where it gets filed — not where it gets captured.

I didn't design the pattern. I found it — by reading my transcripts back.17 / 36

The one doc
I read line
by line.

//

Everything else is generated and refreshed on a cadence. I keep it honest.claude.md, changelog, handoffs — I manage them, I don't type them

//

The plan, I read task by task, phase by phase.

//

Because it's where I decide what gets built, in what order — and which model builds it.assigned in the plan, confirmed in the picker — my call, learned from my engineers and my own digging

//

A phase isn't done until its exit checklist says so.

I don't write the code. I decide who does.22 / 36
Writing for MachinesThe rule§07 / done vs. explored
TRUTH

Done

changelog/ · commits
  • What shipped, when, which files
  • Written automatically, every commit
  • Past tense. Non-negotiable.
HYPOTHESIS

Explored

docs/ · PRDs
  • What I'm considering, testing, arguing with myself about
  • Written by hand, deliberately
  • Future tense. Disposable.

Mix them, and you've handed your teammate contradictory instructions.A human pushes back. An agent just agrees — confidently, in both directions.

Writing for MachinesThe ritual§07 / phase → phase
Phase 1→ HANDOFF.md→ Phase 2
//

Every phase boundary gets a handoff file. Discovery → build. Build → polish.a recent addition — the surface handoff came first

//

The next phase doesn't inherit the history. It inherits the briefing.

//

A new session is a new teammate. Brief it like one.

Not a summary of what happened. A briefing for what's next.24 / 36
Writing for MachinesThe ritual§07 / surface ↔ surface
Claude Chat↔ HANDOFF.md↔ Claude Code
//

Chat → Code. Code → Chat. Both directions, every time.

//

The file is the only thing that crosses. Nothing else survives the hop.

//

Handoff stopped being a cost. It became a ritual.

I don't move surfaces until the handoff is solid. That's the rule.25 / 36

Writing for MachinesOpen source§09 / six skills, all live
// set up the repo — start here
repo-setup
Scaffolds the context stack — concepts, PRDs, decisions, handoffs, changelog. Surveys what you already have, adopts your folder names, never moves or overwrites a thing.
// conventions
branch-naming
Follows your project's convention — read from CLAUDE.md, or inferred.
// what actually shipped?
changelog-tracker
One file per commit. Every fact comes from git.
// why did we choose that?
decisions-logger
Writes each as an ADR. Where the reasoning was never written down, it asks.
// where did we leave off?
handoff-generator
Bidirectional Chat ↔ Code brief. Interviews you first.
// why those three
Changelog. Decisions. Handoff. — the three questions a teammate with amnesia will ask.
// conventions
model-strategy
Which model for which work — with a mandatory review rule.
This repo runs on its own skills. The ADRs, the changelog, the handoffs — all written by the tools. Read the output before you install anything.31 / 36

Writing for MachinesThe lesson§10 / the lesson

Don't say it
twice.
Write it down.

//

No amount of prompting fixes a missing fact.

//

If you're repeating yourself, that's a file you haven't written.

//

Ask what a new teammate would need. Write that.

Writing for Machines§10 / the close

There are two ways to read a codebase: the code, or the decisions.
I can only read one. So I made that one better.The agent got faster. The code got easier.
None of it was a coding problem.
